The prefix overwrite and the primitive projection act on the seam, and each costs under a millisecond on this board. Ten Euler steps are kept until the contraction passes its threshold, because the saving from two steps is small next to the vision cost. Exact guidance, speculative selection and adaptive length, however, all pay for N chunks in series on a sequential engine. Anyone running one of them on an edge board should first check whether the engine samples in a batch, since ours does not. This version covers offline effects and latency only, while the closed-loop columns on the arm, for seam smoothing and for the overwrite in the robot client, belong to a longer version.

Several training-free chunking tricks for flow-matching VLAs came out this year, and their numbers come from desktop or data-centre GPUs (RTX 4090, A100, H100, RTX 5090). On these a chunk costs barely tens of milliseconds and spare compute is plentiful. A robot people can buy runs its policy on an edge GPU. There most of the chunk goes to the vision encoder, which these tricks don't affect. We measured how much of each trick is left on such a board.

Several training-free chunking tricks for flow-matching VLAs came out this year, but their numbers come from desktop or data-centre GPUs (RTX 4090, A100, H100, RTX 5090), where a chunk costs barely tens of milliseconds and spare compute is plentiful. A robot people can buy runs its policy on an edge GPU instead, and there most of the chunk goes to the vision encoder, which these tricks don't affect. We therefore measured how much of each trick is left on such a board.

Two tricks sample several chunks per decision. Speculative chunk selection [arXiv:2610.28019] samples four candidates.
It uses the pre-commit frame to pick the one closest to the recorded teleoperation continuation. Offline it beats a
random pick (one continuation per frame, training-set episodes, open loop). Its paper promises no added control-step
delay. On the Orin, vla.cpp samples the candidates in sequence. A cycle costs {{pact_ms}} ms and {{pact_d}} control
ticks, against {{naive_d}} for a naive chunk (Fig. 3). Entropy-adaptive chunk length [arXiv:2604.04161] samples 20
chunks per decision. One decision takes {{aac_n20_ms}} ms on the Orin. The threshold was {{aac_bar_ms}} ms. The chosen
length also sits at the floor in both task phases. The jump is no better than with fixed chunks and the overwrite.

Two tricks sample several chunks per decision. Speculative chunk selection [arXiv:2610.28019] samples four candidates and, using the pre-commit frame, picks the one closest to the recorded teleoperation continuation. Offline it beats a random pick (one continuation per frame, training-set episodes, open loop), and its paper promises no added control-step delay. On the Orin, however, vla.cpp samples the candidates in sequence, so a cycle costs {{pact_ms}} ms and {{pact_d}} control ticks against {{naive_d}} for a naive chunk (Fig. 3). Entropy-adaptive chunk length [arXiv:2604.04161] samples 20 chunks per decision, and one decision takes {{aac_n20_ms}} ms on the Orin against a threshold of {{aac_bar_ms}} ms. The chosen length also sits at the floor in both task phases, and the jump is no better than with fixed chunks and the overwrite.

Our robot is an SO-101 arm [arXiv:2606.08881] with a Jetson Orin NX 16 GB. It runs SmolVLA [arXiv:2506.01844] through
vla.cpp, a C++ inference engine, on episodes recorded with LeRobot. This paper started once SmolVLA ran on the arm
through vla.cpp. We then looked at where the rest of a chunk's time went, and at which published tricks could still
help. We took seven of them. Each one is a gate with a bar committed before the number. Offline effects get an episode
bootstrap, and latencies are medians of at least 50 calls. The appendix maps every number to its result file and
protocol commit.

Two works use the same arm to evaluate policies. One is a standardized real-world benchmark that reports a taxonomy of failures and recoveries for VLA policies [@2606.08881]. The other runs a fleet of SO-101 cells and evaluates policies at scale [@2607.24481]. The vla-eval tool runs VLAs across 14 simulation benchmarks [@2603.13966], and a benchmark of demonstration quality studies one method family [@2610.18869]. We do something different. We test the claims behind methods (judges, world models, latency) against thresholds fixed before the run, and we audit our own pre-registration. The closest work is RoboSeed [@2610.40026]. It scores VLA and world-action models on five dimensions, including reproduction evidence and deployment affordability. The reproduction-evidence score counts five audit milestones: configuration mapping, task records, task coverage, training records and seeds. Its authors state that the score is not a probability that a result is correct. We give one pass or fail per claim on a €{{rig_eur}} rig.

The early gates mixed point estimates and different intervals. We recomputed {{rc_rows}} of them from stored rows with one statistic, the episode bootstrap ({{rc_resamples}} resamples, percentile 95 % CI). For {{rc_flips}} of them the bar falls inside the interval (Table 2). The colour judge is a {{acc_verdict}} on the point estimate, and its interval does not settle it. The false-intervention threshold was fitted to meet its rate, so that interval is only descriptive. The register keeps the pre-registered point verdicts and marks these three as fragile.
